short: Scottish pikemen broke an English army and made independence a fact on the ground.
full:
On 23 and 24 June 1314 Robert the Bruce met Edward II of England on wet, broken ground near the Bannock Burn, south of Stirling. Edward had marched north to relieve Stirling Castle, whose governor had agreed to surrender if not relieved by midsummer. On the first day the Scots held the approaches and Bruce killed Sir Henry de Bohun in single combat with an axe.

On the second day Bruce did what Scottish commanders had avoided since Falkirk: he advanced his schiltrons, dense formations of long spears, against the English as they deployed on cramped ground between watercourses. The cavalry could not manoeuvre and the archers could not be brought to bear. The English line collapsed and thousands were killed or drowned; Edward escaped to Dunbar. The war ran on until the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton in 1328, but Bannockburn secured Bruce's throne. Sabaton's "Blood of Bannockburn", from The Last Stand (2016), tells it from the Scottish side.
